prompt: In many communities, local charities and clubs are finding it increasingly difficult to recruit volunteers. Why is this happening? What could be done to encourage more people to give their time?
essay:
Many local organisations, from sports clubs to food banks, say that volunteers are becoming harder to find. In my view the main reasons lie in how people now work and live, and the most effective response is for organisations to change what they ask of volunteers.

The first reason is time, but not simply in the sense that people are busier. Growing numbers of workers have irregular hours, shift patterns that change from week to week, or more than one job, and this makes it difficult to promise to be somewhere every Tuesday evening. A second factor is mobility. People who expect to move for work within few years have less reason to become attached to a particular neighbourhood, and the informal networks through which volunteers were traditionally recruited — a word from a neighbour, a notice outside a place of worship — reach fewer of them. Finally, volunteering itself has become more demanding, with training courses, background checks and forms that can discourage someone who only wanted to help.

Several measures could reverse this trend. Organisations could offer shorter and more flexible roles, such as helping at a single event, instead of relying on long-term commitments that many people can no longer make. Employers could give staff a small number of paid volunteering days each year, which would ease the time pressure directly. Governments could also simplify the checks required for low-risk roles, while keeping them in place where people work with children or vulnerable adults.

In short, people have not become less generous; their lives have become less predictable. If voluntary organisations adapt to that, rather than waiting for the committed weekly volunteer to return, they are likely to find more help than they expect.
title: Why local charities struggle to find volunteers
